name: Retainers

lead: Retainers keep a smile straight after braces or aligners by holding teeth in their corrected positions so they do not drift back.

Teeth can relapse because of gum fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued jaw growth. Types include Hawley retainers (wire and acrylic), clear vacuum-formed trays and wires bonded behind the front teeth. On looksmaxxing forums some users ask whether retainers restrict palate growth or undo mewing; no studies cited here address that.

paras: Fixed retainers stay bonded and work continuously, while removable ones are worn as instructed, often full time at first and then at night. How long they are worn is set by the treating orthodontist and may be indefinite.

Reported problems include decay when clear retainers are worn while eating or drinking sugary fluids, plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned, speech effects from Hawley designs, breakage and warping.

angle.text: Retainers keep a smile straight after braces or aligners by holding teeth where they were moved, which limits relapse. Looksmaxxing forums also ask whether retainers affect palate or jaw development; no studies cited here test that.

lead: Orthodontic retainers are appliances worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their corrected positions. Teeth can drift back toward their former positions (relapse) because of recoil of gum fibers, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued jaw growth.[1]

Common types are Hawley retainers (a wire and acrylic palate plate), vacuum-formed clear retainers, and fixed retainers bonded behind the teeth. How long they are worn is set by the treating orthodontist and may be indefinite.[1]

In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are also discussed in connection with mewing and jaw or palate development, with some users asking whether wearing them could restrict maxillary growth. No studies cited here test that question.

paras: A Hawley retainer is a wire running across the front teeth anchored in an acrylic palate plate; it is adjustable and one of the oldest designs, named for Charles A. Hawley. Reported drawbacks include appearance, effect on speech, fracture risk and weaker control of the lower front teeth.[1] Acrylic (polymethyl methacrylate) is widely used in prosthodontics and in making orthodontic retainers.[2]

Vacuum-formed retainers are clear shells over the whole arch; they are less visible and cheaper and are usually worn overnight. Fixed retainers are wires bonded to the back of the front teeth, usually the six front teeth or just the canines, and need less patient cooperation but are harder to clean.[1] Begg, Barrer and app-linked retainers also exist.[1] Direct-bonded retainers were described in the clinical literature by the 1970s.[3]

Retainers rely on gum fibers adapting to the new tooth position, which is why relapse can occur if they are not worn as directed. Fixed retainers are described as performing best for holding the lower incisors, with vacuum-formed retainers better than other removable types.[1]

Vacuum-formed retainers worn while eating or after sugary drinks can trap sugars against the teeth, and can break in people who grind their teeth. Hawley retainers can affect speech, and poorly cleaned retainers of any type can lead to plaque, cavities and gum inflammation. Very hot water can warp removable retainers.[1]

Users on looksmax.org have started threads asking whether retainers stop or reduce palate growth in teenagers, whether wearing them undoes mewing progress, and what to do with retainers after treatment.[4][5][6] One poster who had clear aligners at about age 11 or 12 wrote that years in a retainer sized for a younger child may have left the upper jaw behind the lower, and described stopping the retainer and adding mewing and chewing.[4] Others discuss wearing retainers to keep teeth stable before planned jaw surgery.[7]

No studies found on retainers and facial or palatal growth. Clinical reports of retainers concern tooth stability and hygiene; early clinical experience with direct-bonded retainers was reported in 1977.[3]

lore.intro: Retainer threads on looksmax.org mostly ask whether routine post-braces retainers conflict with mewing, jaw growth or planned expansion surgery.[4][5][6]
